title: Seven of Wands Tarot Card Meaning: Upright, Reversed & Love
description: Seven of Wands upright: standing your ground, conviction; reversed: worn down, giving in. Love, work, advice and Waite's 1911 words. Ask your question.
h1: Seven of Wands Tarot Card Meaning
image_alt: Seven of Wands, 1909 Rider–Waite–Smith card: a young man in green on a rise swings a staff as six staves rise toward him from below.
capsule: The Seven of Wands stands for standing your ground: defending a position, an idea or your boundaries under pressure, with conviction. Reversed, it can mean feeling worn down, giving in or getting defensive. It is a demanding but brave card. Since the contest on the hill is still going on, it is not clear yet which way the answer falls.

blocks.heading: What is on the Seven of Wands card?
paragraphs: A young man stands on high ground and swings a staff while six others rise toward him from below. Waite's description: "A young man on a craggy eminence brandishing a staff; six other staves are raised towards him from below" (p. 184). His own staff, held across his body with both hands, is the largest thing on the card.

On the 1909 card he wears a green tunic and stands with his feet wide apart on a green rise edged with rock. The six staves rise from the bottom edge in front of him, none of them higher than his waist. His feet do not match: a low shoe on one, an ankle boot on the other. VII is printed at the top.

blocks.heading: What did Waite write about the Seven of Wands?
paragraphs: Waite reads it as "a card of valour, for, on the surface, six are attacking one, who has, however, the vantage position" (p. 184). Waite adds that on the level of ideas it means discussion and "wordy strife" (p. 184).

It is also, Waite writes, a card of success, because the man on top may be out of his opponents' reach (p. 184). On the reversed side, Waite's perplexity and anxiety end with a caution against indecision (p. 184).

blocks.heading: What does the Seven of Wands mean upright?
paragraphs: Holding your position under pressure is the core of the Seven of Wands: defending an idea in a meeting, keeping a boundary when others push, staying with a choice that people question. It is a card of conviction and challenge, and of the courage to stay put.

The high ground matters. You may have an advantage, in knowledge, experience or simply a clear sense of what you want, but keeping it takes energy and focus. Not every challenge needs an answer, though.
Stand firm where it truly matters to you, and stop defending what you no longer care about.

blocks.heading: What does the Seven of Wands mean reversed?
paragraphs: Turned over, the card can show someone worn down by constant defending and tempted to give in just to end the pressure. Giving in is not always wrong, but check whether you are choosing it or are simply too tired to choose.

The other side is defensiveness: treating every comment as an attack and fighting battles nobody started. Waite's caution against indecision (p. 184) fits both cases; tiredness and defensiveness are modern readings. Ask which ground is truly yours, and protect that with calm rather than exhaustion.

blocks.heading: What does the Seven of Wands mean in love?
paragraphs: Protecting what you have is the love theme here: guarding a relationship against outside pressure, family opinions or a rival, and standing up for your own needs inside it. Holding your ground can be calm and gentle rather than a fight.
While dating, the card can describe keeping your standards when others suggest you lower them, or holding on to a boundary you set early.
Upside down, it may show tiredness from always having to justify yourself, or a guardedness that keeps closeness away. Where are you defending yourself out of habit?

blocks.heading: What does the Seven of Wands mean for work and money?
paragraphs: Other candidates for the same role, a crowded market, a decision you have to defend in front of colleagues: competition runs through this card's work meaning. Waite himself lists negotiations, trade rivalry, barter and competition for business (p. 184). Your position is strong if you prepare well and keep your arguments short.
Money-wise, the Seven of Wands means protecting what you have earned: guarding a budget against pressure to spend, holding your price, defending your share in a competitive field.

blocks.heading: What is the advice of the Seven of Wands?
paragraphs: Decide which one position you will keep and which you are willing to let go. Then hold the first one calmly: state it once, clearly, without raising your voice. Being firm does not mean answering every challenge.

blocks.heading: Is the Seven of Wands a yes or no card?
The Seven of Wands as a person and as feelings
paragraphs: On the high ground with his staff, the Seven of Wands is principled and protective: someone who speaks up, holds a line and can turn stubborn when pushed. As feelings, it means a protective, determined stance: wanting to keep the bond safe and caring enough to stand up for it, along with some guardedness, holding back until trust feels solid. Reversed, the feelings may be weariness, doubt about whether the effort is worth it, or a defensive streak that pushes the other person away.

blocks.heading: The Seven of Wands with other cards

pairs.text: Many small disputes; decide which one deserves your defense.
Firmness with a gentle hand: calm courage holds better than force.
Defending too much at once. Put down what is not yours to carry.
Unsure what to defend. Make the choice, then stand by it.

blocks.heading: Seven of Wands or Nine of Wands?
paragraphs: Waite's Nine of Wands shows a figure who "leans upon his staff and has an expectant look, as if awaiting an enemy" (p. 180), with eight staves standing behind him like a fence; today it is read as resilience and the last stretch of a long effort. The Seven is the active defense, with the challenge in front of you. The Nine is the pause after many rounds, tired but still watchful.

blocks.heading: Questions to ask yourself about the Seven of Wands
paragraphs: What position am I defending right now, and do I still believe in it?
Where am I being defensive when nobody is attacking?
What would standing my ground calmly look like here?

faq.q: Is the Seven of Wands a good or bad card?
faq.a: Mostly good, though tiring. It shows you holding an advantage under pressure, which takes courage and gives you a real chance to keep your place. The cost is energy, since constant defense wears anyone out. Reversed, it asks whether this particular fight is still worth it.

faq.q: Does the Seven of Wands mean I have enemies?
faq.a: No. Waite does describe six attacking one (p. 184), but modern readings treat the staves as pressure: criticism, competition, demands or doubts, sometimes your own. The card speaks about how you respond, not about who is against you.

faq.q: Why does the man on the Seven of Wands wear mismatched shoes?
faq.a: Waite does not say; his description of the picture never mentions the shoes (p. 184). On the 1909 card one foot has a low shoe and the other a boot. A common modern explanation is that he had to get ready in a hurry, which suits a challenge that came without warning.

waite.quote: It is a card of valour … It is further a card of success … Reversed: Perplexity, embarrassments, anxiety. It is also a caution against indecision.
